title: Linux Foundation CKS
summary: The Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS) is an advanced, performance-based certification that proves a candidate can secure containerised workloads and the Kubernetes clusters that run them. It is intended for engineers who already administer Kubernetes competently and now carry responsibility for its security posture: platform engineers, DevSecOps practitioners, cloud security architects and incident responders who operate clusters in regulated or internet-facing environments. Unlike an entry-level associate exam, the CKS assumes fluency in cluster operations and tests judgment under constraints, so it is normally taken by people who have held a Kubernetes administration credential or equivalent production experience. To an employer the credential is evidence that the holder can harden a cluster end to end: restrict the API server and its components, enforce admission control, lock down network paths, reduce container privilege, protect the software supply chain from build through deploy, and detect and investigate suspicious runtime behaviour. The examination is entirely practical, taken in a live cluster environment where candidates solve real configuration and investigation tasks; because scoring depends on the actual state of the cluster, an answer that is conceptually right but not applied correctly earns nothing. Documentation is available during the session, so memorisation matters far less than speed and accuracy of hands-on work. Practice therefore dominates outcomes. Candidates who repeatedly build a cluster, break a control, and verify with read-only inspection commands develop the reflex to confirm every change, which is exactly what the exam rewards and what real incident work demands. Only defensive technique is relevant here: every control in scope exists to reduce attacker freedom.
objectives: Cluster Setup: harden cluster components, restrict network access to the control plane, apply CIS-style benchmark checks and verify the resulting configuration.
Cluster Hardening: manage role-based access control tightly, limit service account permissions, and understand how API server flags and admission controls interact.
System Hardening: minimise the host attack surface, constrain IAM and node access, and reason about the trade-off between usability and least privilege.
Minimise Microservice Vulnerabilities: apply security contexts, pod security admission, sealed secrets and runtime sandboxing to reduce container breakout risk.
Supply Chain Security: verify image provenance and integrity, sign and scan artefacts, and enforce policy over what may be deployed into the cluster.
Monitoring, Logging and Runtime Security: enable audit logging, detect behavioural anomalies in workloads, and investigate compromised containers with immutable evidence.
Network Security: write and test network policies, secure ingress paths, and reason about segmentation between namespaces and tenants.
Secrets and Configuration Management: store and rotate sensitive material safely, and avoid exposing credentials through environment variables or mounted files.
Incident Response in Kubernetes: isolate a suspect workload, preserve forensic artefacts, and recover a cluster without destroying evidence.

beginner.definition: The Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist is an advanced, hands-on certification about securing Kubernetes. Kubernetes is a system that runs software in containers across many machines. The exam tests whether you can harden a real cluster, restrict what each part may do, and investigate suspicious activity. It assumes you already administer Kubernetes well.
beginner.whyItMatters: A cluster runs many pieces of software for many teams. One weak container can give an attacker a foothold inside everything else. Default settings are often too open, because they favour convenience over safety. This certification teaches you to close those gaps, limit movement between workloads, and prove your changes took effect. That last habit matters most in real work.
howItWorks: You lock down the cluster control plane, which is the part that gives orders to everything else.
You tighten permissions, so each user and service can only do the small job it needs.
You reduce container privilege, so a broken program cannot escape and harm the host machine.
You check software before it is deployed, by verifying where each image came from.
You switch on logging and watch running workloads for behaviour that looks wrong.
beginner.example: Think of a large apartment building. Every tenant has a key to their own flat, not to the whole building. The main door, the lift and the shared boiler room each have their own rules. If one tenant leaves their door open, the neighbours should still be safe. A weak cluster is a building where every key opens every door. The specialist's job is to cut new keys, check who holds them, and watch the cameras.
takeaways: Least privilege means every part gets only the access it truly needs.
Verify with a read-only command after every change you make.
Default settings favour convenience, so review them before you trust them.
